standard_prerequisites.name: Truncation and its induction principle
standard_prerequisites.statement: \trunc n A is the n-truncation of A with \tproj n{\blank} : A \to \trunc n A, and it is universal among n-truncated types.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the operation whose interaction with path types is computed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Encode-decode method
standard_prerequisites.statement: To show a map into a path type of a truncated type is an equivalence, generalise the two endpoints and build a family P on the truncation together with maps decode and encode that are inverse to each other.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the method the whole proof follows (source lines 677-679).

standard_prerequisites.name: Level of a type of truncated types
standard_prerequisites.statement: The type \typele{n} of n-truncated types is itself (n+1)-truncated, so a family with values in it can be defined by induction from its value at the base point.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the justification that P is well defined (source line 686).

core_obligations: Generalise the map to a family P over two truncation variables by setting P(\tproj{n+1}x, \tproj{n+1}y) \defeq \trunc n{x=_A y} and check that the definition is legitimate because \trunc n{x=_A y} and \typele{n} have the required truncation levels (source lines 681-686).
Define decode : P(u,v) \to (u = v) on the generators and use n-truncatedness of the codomain to define it by induction on u and v (source lines 688-693).
Define r : \prd{u} P(u,u) by induction on the truncation, with r(\tproj{n+1}x) \defeq \tproj n{\refl x}, and encode(p) \defeq transport of r(u) along p (source lines 695-703).

Show the composite decode \circ encode is the identity by path induction, reducing to decode(r(u)) = \refl u and then, since the goal is an (n-1)-type, to the defining equations of r and decode (source lines 705-710).

Show the composite encode \circ decode is the identity by reducing to the case of the generators and computing the transport of \tproj n{\refl x} along ap(\tproj{n+1})(p) in five steps (source lines 712-720).

proof_roadmap.step: Introduce the encode-decode method and define the generalised family P by truncation induction.
Define decode on generators and r and encode by transport.
Check the first composite by path induction, using that the goal is an (n-1)-type.
Check the second composite by a five-step transport computation, then specialise to the two projected endpoints.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled theorem at source lines 671-674 (book Theorem 7.3.12): for every A, x, y : A and n \ge -2 the map of equation eq:path-trunc-map is an equivalence, so \trunc n{x=_A y} is equivalent to the path type of \trunc{n+1}A between the two projections. The statement records only that equivalence, while the proof (source lines 676-722) has to run the encode-decode method in full: it generalises the two endpoints to arbitrary elements of \trunc{n+1}A through a family P whose very well-definedness is an application of the level result thm:hleveln-of-hlevelSn, defines decode on the generators and justifies that by n-truncatedness of the codomain, builds r by induction on the truncation, defines encode by transporting r along the given path, and then verifies both composites: the first reduces by path induction to an equation whose goal is an (n-1)-type, the second needs the five-step computation that moves the transport of \tproj n{\refl x} along ap(\tproj{n+1})(p) through the truncation and the path family, using thm:transport-compose and thm:ap-transport. There is no way to induct on an equality between two projections, which is exactly why the generalisation is unavoidable.
